text:
Mark your calendar: TRICARE Open Season runs Nov. 9–Dec. 8, 2026, and it's your one yearly chance to change health plans without a life event.

It applies if you have or qualify for TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select. You can stay in your plan, enroll or switch, including between individual and family enrollment. It doesn't apply to active duty, TRICARE For Life, Reserve Select, Retired Reserve or Young Adult.

Dental and vision run on a separate schedule. Federal Benefits Open Season for FEDVIP is Nov. 9–Dec. 14, and you'll need a TRICARE health plan for vision.

All changes take effect Jan. 1, 2027. Enroll through milConnect, by phone or by mail. Swipe through, then check DEERS so your info is current.

title: Welter v. Defense Health Agency | District Court, District of Columbia | Tracelaw Court Monitor
description:
1 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA 2 PAUL WELTER, et al., Plaintiffs, V. 3 DEFENSE HEALTH AGENCY, Defendant.
23-cv-926, 2026 WL 585104, at *1 (D.D.C.
18-cv-140, 2023 WL 6199075, at *7 n.5 (D.D.C.
23-cv-2112, 2026 WL 775907, at *6 (D.D.C.
2d 134, 144 (D.D.C.
text:
1

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

2

PAUL WELTER, et al., Plaintiffs, V.

3

DEFENSE HEALTH AGENCY, Defendant.

4

Civil Action No. 25 - 2875 (SLS)

5

Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan

6

MEMORANDUM OPINION

7

In this Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) case, Paul and Teresa Welter seek a single investigative report from the Defense Health Agency (DHA) concerning suspected medical abuse of the Welters' two minor daughters. DHA produced the report with significant redactions, relying on FOIA Exemptions 3, 5, 6, and 7(C) to justify its withholdings. Both sides now seek summary judgment. The Court grants in part and denies in part both motions. DHA may not withhold the report in full under Exemption 3, but it has justified its redactions under Exemptions 5, 6, and 7(C).

8

BACKGROUND

9

A. Statutory Background

10

"FOIA 'implement[s] a general philosophy of full agency disclosure." Informed Consent Action Network v. NIH, No. 23-cv-926, 2026 WL 585104, at *1 (D.D.C. Mar. 3, 2026) (alteration in original) (quoting DOJ v. Reps. Comm. for Freedom of the Press, 489 U.S. 749, 754 (1989)).

11

The statute "requires every federal agency, upon request, to make 'promptly available to any person' any 'records' so long as the request 'reasonably describes such records."" Assassination Archives & Rsch. Ctr. v. CIA, 334 F.3d 55, 57 (D.C. Cir. 2003) (quoting 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3)(A)). "Agencies must construe FOIA requests liberally and can only withhold or redact documents if

12

the information requested 'falls within one of nine statutory exemptions." Informed Consent Action Network, 2026 WL 585104, at *1 (quoting People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) v. NIH, 745 F.3d 535, 540 (D.C. Cir. 2014)); see 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(1)-(9). These exemptions demonstrate that the public's right to information is "not absolute and that disclosure of certain information may harm legitimate governmental or private interests[.]" Martin v. DOJ, 488 F.3d 446, 453 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (cleaned up). The agency bears the burden of establishing that an exemption applies and ordinarily "must disclose all reasonably segregable, nonexempt portions of the requested record(s)." PETA, 745 F.3d at 540 (cleaned up). And the agency must show that it "reasonably foresees that disclosure would harm an interest protected by" one of FOIA's nine exemptions or that disclosure is otherwise prohibited by law. [5] U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(i).

13

[5] Under FOIA, an agency may "withhold information ... only if the agency reasonably foresees that disclosure would harm an interest protected by an exemption." 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(i)(I). The foreseeable-harm requirement does not apply to Exemption 3. See id. § 552(a)(8)(B); Leopold v. DOJ, 94 F.4th 33, 37 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (explaining that Congress's 2016 addition of the foreseeable-harm requirement "limited withholding pursuant to all exemptions, except Exemption 3"). And the Welters do not contest DHA's showing on foreseeable harm for any of its withholdings under Exemptions 5, 6, and 7(C). See generally Mot. (not addressing foreseeable harm); Reply & Cross-Opp'n (same). On this record, the Court is satisfied that DHA has carried its burden. See, e.g., Lahiff Decl. 129 (attesting that in the context of child-abuse and sexual-assault investigations, the public availability of AFCCP reports "would most certainly impact AFCCP's ability to offer frank and honest opinions and recommendations to help those that would rely on them the most-abused children"); id. 135 (stating that the release of the identities of "alleged child victims" in "the context of these investigative records would cause embarrassment, as well as unsolicited and unnecessary attention to be focused on these individuals" and "could force them to relive emotionally trying events, causing further invasion of their privacy, in excess of the harm they may have already endured"); Withholding Mem. at 9-10 (describing harms from disclosure to the Welters' children and AFCCP and CID staff).

14

B. Factual and Procedural Background

15

The Court draws the facts from the Parties' Statements of Material Facts and the underlying materials referenced in those statements. See Pls.' Statement of Undisputed Facts (PSOF), ECF No. 17-1; Def.'s Statement of Undisputed Material Facts (DSOF), ECF No. 21-3. The Court assumes the facts in those statements to be true unless they have been specifically disputed, and it assumes the truth of other undisputed statements in the record. See Fed.

16

R. Civ. P. 56(e)(2); see

17

also LCvR 7(h)(1).[1]

18

[1] Local Rule 7(h) provides that "the Court may assume that facts identified by the moving party in its statement of material facts are admitted, unless such a fact is controverted in the statement of genuine issues filed in opposition to the motion." LCvR 7(h)(1).

19

In November 2020, Teresa Welter reported to the Army's Criminal Investigative Division (CID) that one of her minor daughters may have been sexually abused by a Department of Defense Education Agency (DODEA) contractor tasked with transporting the child to and from school in Stuttgart, Germany. PSOF 11. A month later, Dr. Brian Brennan, a pediatrician affiliated with the

20

Armed Forces Center for Child Protection (AFCCP), produced a 14-page report "render[ing] an opinion" on whether Mrs. Welter herself had medically abused her two daughters. See Redacted Report, Pls.' Ex. 3, ECF No. 17-2; PSOF 12; Decl. of Patrick L. Lahiff (Lahiff Decl.) 11 6-10, ECF No. 21-4. The Air Force then investigated the Welters for medical abuse of their daughters.

21

PSOF 111.

22

In April 2025, the Welters submitted a FOIA request to DHA-the federal agency responsible for, among other things, overseeing military health care facilities, see 10 U.S.C.

23

§ 1073c(b)-seeking Dr. Brennan's report, PSOF 116; DSOF 121. The Welters ultimately filed

24

a FOIA suit to obtain the document. Compl. 119-13, ECF No. 1. In January 2026, DHA produced the report with extensive withholdings under FOIA Exemptions 3, 5, 6, and 7(C). See PSOF 11 18- 19; DSOF 11 27, 31. And in April 2026, DHA produced a withholding memorandum-in lieu of a Vaughn index-to justify its withholdings. See Withholding Mem., Pls.' Ex. 5, ECF No. 17-4;

25

PSOF 1 20. The Parties now cross-move for summary judgment. See Pls.' Mot. Summ. J. (Mot.), ECF No. 17; Def.'s Opp'n & Cross-Mot. Summ. J. (Opp'n & Cross-Mot.), ECF No. 21-2; Pls.'

26

Reply & Cross-Opp'n (Reply & Cross-Opp'n), ECF No. 23; Def.'s Cross-Reply (Cross-Reply), ECF No. 24. Those motions are ripe for review.[2]

27

[2] The Welters' summary-judgment motion briefly argues that the withheld report must also be released under the Privacy Act. See Mot. at 13-14. But any Privacy Act claim is not properly before the Court. The Welters' Complaint pleads only a single FOIA violation, Compl. 11 9-13, and they "cannot amend their complaint through summary-judgment briefing[,]" Barot v. Aldon Mgmt., No. 18-cv-140, 2023 WL 6199075, at *7 n.5 (D.D.C. Sep. 22, 2023) (cleaned up).

28

LEGAL STANDARD

29

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56 requires a court to "grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." Fed.

30

R. Civ. P. 56(a). In a FOIA suit, an agency is entitled to

31

summary judgment if it establishes that "no material facts are in dispute" and that all information subject to a request has either "been produced or is wholly exempt from the Act's inspection requirements." Students Against Genocide v. Dep't of State, 257 F.3d 828, 833 (D.C. Cir. 2001) (cleaned up).

32

Typically, an "agency demonstrates the applicability of a FOIA exemption by providing affidavits regarding the claimed exemptions." Shapiro v. DOJ, 893 F.3d 796, 799 (D.C. Cir. 2018). "If an agency's affidavit describes the justifications for withholding the information with specific detail, demonstrates that the information withheld logically falls within the claimed exemption, and is not contradicted by contrary evidence in the record or by evidence of the agency's bad faith, then summary judgment is warranted on the basis of the affidavit alone." ACLU v. DOD, 628 F.3d 612, 619 (D.C. Cir. 2011). "[A]n agency's justification for invoking a FOIA exemption is sufficient if it appears 'logical' or 'plausible." Wolf v. CIA, 473 F.3d 370, 374-75 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (quoting Gardels v. CIA, 689 F.2d 1100, 1105 (D.C. Cir. 1982)).

33

DISCUSSION

34

DHA invokes FOIA Exemption 3 to withhold Dr. Brennan's report in full, and it justifies redactions of the report under Exemptions 5, 6, and 7(C). The Court considers each exemption in turn, ultimately concluding that DHA fails to meet its burden on Exemption 3 but properly invokes Exemptions 5, 6, and 7(C).

35

A. Exemption 3

36

First up is Exemption 3, which DHA claims allows it to withhold Dr. Brennan's report in full. Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 5. Exemption 3 applies to records that are "specifically exempted from disclosure by statute" so long as that statute either "requires that the matters be withheld from the public in such a manner as to leave no discretion on the issue" or "establishes particular criteria

37

for withholding or refers to particular types of matters to be withheld."3 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(3)(A). "To withhold records under Exemption 3, an agency must make two showings: that the statute is one of exemption as contemplated by Exemption 3, and that the withheld material falls within the statute." Corley v. DOJ, 998 F.3d 981, 984-85 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (cleaned up).

38

Here, DHA relies on the Child Victims' Act to justify withholding Dr. Brennan's report under Exemption 3. See Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 4 (citing 18 U.S.C. § 3509(d)(1)). Both Parties agree that the Act is a qualifying Exemption 3 statute. See Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 5; Reply & Cross-Opp'n at 1; see also Corley, 998 F.3d at 985 (holding that "the Child Victims' Act unambiguously qualifies as an Exemption 3 statute"). So the validity of DHA's Exemption 3 withholding turns on whether the report falls within the ambit of the Child Victims' Act.

39

The Child Victims' Act applies to children "who [are] or [are] alleged to be .. . a victim of a crime of physical abuse, sexual abuse, or exploitation" or "a witness to a crime committed against another person[.]" 18 U.S.C. § 3509(a)(2). The Act imposes a duty of confidentiality on "all employees of the Government" when "acting ... in connection with a criminal proceeding[.]" Id.

40

§ 3509(d)(1)(A), (B)(i). It requires covered government personnel to:

41

(i) keep all documents that disclose the name or any other information concerning

42

a child in a secure place to which no person who does not have reason to know their contents has access; and (ii) disclose documents described in clause (i) or the information in them that concerns a child only to persons who, by reason of their participation in the proceeding, have reason to know such information.

43

Id. §3509(d)(1)(A)(i)-(ii). Thus, to withhold a document under the Act, an agency must show that that the document was (1) collected or generated "in connection with a criminal proceeding," and

44

(2) "disclose[s] the name or any other information concerning a child[.]" 18 U.S.C.

45

§ 3509(d)(1)(A), (A)(i).

46

Beginning with the first prong, "[t]he term 'criminal proceeding' is not defined in the Child Victims['] Act." Mid-Atl. Innocence Project v. FBI, No. 23-cv-2112, 2026 WL 775907, at *6 (D.D.C. Mar. 19, 2026). And the Parties read that term differently. DHA contends that the term "criminal proceeding" includes a federal investigation into "allegations of child abuse ... and sexual assault[.]" Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 7-8. The Welters counter that it requires a "judicial" proceeding. See Mot. at 5-6; Reply & Cross-Opp'n at 2-4. The Court concludes that the Welters have the better reading. An agency invoking Subsection 3509(d) of the Child Victims' Act to withhold records under Exemption 3 must show that the records relate to a judicial proceeding. "Absent a reason to think otherwise, [courts] interpret statutory terms according to the ordinary meanings they had when they were enacted." USPS v. Konan, 607 U.S. 391, 399 (2026). "To determine the ordinary meaning of a legal term, [courts] may look to contemporaneous dictionaries." Institutional S'holder Servs., Inc. v. SEC, 142 F.4th 757, 766 (D.C. Cir. 2025) (cleaned up). In 1990-when the Child Victims' Act was enacted, see supra note 3-the ordinary meaning of "criminal proceeding" encompassed some form of judicial involvement, rather than a criminal investigation. Dictionaries explained that a criminal proceeding is "[o]ne instituted and conducted for the purpose either of preventing the commission of crime, or for fixing the guilt of a crime already committed and punishing the offender," and clarified that "[s]trictly, a 'criminal proceeding' means some step taken before a court against some person or persons charged with some violation of the criminal law." Criminal Proceeding, Black's Law Dictionary (6th ed. 1990);

47

see also Criminal Proceeding, Ballentine's Law Dictionary (3d ed. 1969) ("A proceeding in court in the prosecution of a person charged or to be charged with the commission of a crime, contemplating the conviction and punishment of the person charged or to be charged."). Thus, a plain reading of Subsection 3509(d) reveals that a criminal investigation does not suffice.

48

The structure of the Child Victims' Act aligns with its text. The Supreme Court has explained that "[i]n a given statute, the same term usually has the same meaning and different terms usually have different meanings." Pulsifer v. United States, 601 U.S. 124, 149 (2024) (citing Antonin Scalia & Bryan Garner, Reading Law at 170-71 (2012)). Here, each of Section 3509's five uses of the term "criminal proceeding" contemplates a judicial proceeding. See 18 U.S.C.

49

§ 3509(k) (A "civil action shall be stayed until the end of all phases of the criminal action and any

50

mention of the civil action during the criminal proceeding is prohibited. As used in this subsection, a criminal action is pending until its final adjudication in the trial court." (emphasis added)); id.

51

§ 3509(m)(1) ("In any criminal proceeding, any property or material that constitutes child

52

pornography ... shall remain in the care, custody, and control of either the Government or the court." (emphasis added)); id. § 3509(m)(2)(A) ("Notwithstanding Rule 16 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, a court shall deny, in any criminal proceeding, any request by the defendant" to reproduce certain material. (emphasis added)); id. § 3509(m)(3) ("In any criminal proceeding, a victim .. . shall have reasonable access to any property or material that constitutes child pornography ... depicting the victim, for inspection, viewing, and examination at a Government facility or court[.]" (emphasis added); see also Mid-Atl. Innocence Project, 2026 WL 775907, at *6 (citing 18 U.S.C. § 3509(d)(1)(A), (k), (m)(1), (m)(2)(A), (m)(3)) (concluding that "[t]he natural reading of 'criminal proceedings' throughout [Section 3509] is that this phrase refers to criminal actions in federal courts").

53

DHA makes three arguments to the contrary, none of which persuade the Court.

54

First, DHA contends that interpreting the Child Victims' Act to exclude investigations "would invert the statute's protective purpose." Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 10. But Congress said otherwise in passing the Child Victims' Act. It explained that "[a]s the number of child abuse cases continues climbing each year, it has become increasingly urgent that America design special procedures to protect child victims and witnesses in court." H.R. Rep. No. 101-681, pt. 1, at 165

55

(1990) (emphasis added). In any event, a statute's purpose cannot supplant its text. See, e.g.,

56

Corner Post, Inc. v. Bd. of Governors of Fed. Rsrv. Sys., 603 U.S. 799, 815 (2024) ("As [the Supreme Court] has repeatedly stated, the text of a law controls over purported legislative intentions unmoored from any statutory text; the Court may not replace the actual text with speculation as to Congress' intent." (cleaned up)). And as explained above, the text of Subsection 3509(d) requires a judicial proceeding. So DHA's purposive argument gets it nowhere.

57

Second, DHA marshals a trio of district court cases to support its broader reading of the Child Victims' Act. See Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 7, 10; Cross-Reply at 4-6. But none of those cases involved the statute's criminal-proceeding requirement. DHA first relies on Radar Online LLC v.

58

FBI, 692 F. Supp. 3d 318 (S.D.N.Y. 2023), where the court sustained the FBI's invocation of Exemption 3 "to protect names, images, and identifying information of minor children victims and witnesses within the child prostitution investigation of Jeffrey Epstein." Id. at 346 (cleaned up).

59

But the court did not analyze the criminal-proceeding requirement of the Child Victims' Act, stating only that the "[p]laintiffs ha[d] not offered any basis to believe that the FBI's justification [was] insufficient." Id. And the FOIA request expressly sought "all documents relating to the FBI's investigation and prosecution" of Mr. Epstein for sex-trafficking crimes, id. at 333 (emphasis

60

added), thus placing the records squarely within the scope of a criminal proceeding covered by the Child Victims' Act.

61

DHA next invokes Habeas Corpus Resource Center v. FBI, No. 22-cv-01086, 2025 WL 3500672 (N.D. Cal. Sep. 30, 2025), where the court upheld the FBI's withholdings of documents "relate[d] to then-ongoing investigations or criminal proceedings regarding crimes against children[.]" Id. at *5. But again, the court did not consider whether the Child Victims' Act could be invoked in the absence of criminal proceedings. Rather, it grappled with an argument that "the information regarding children remains confidential and exempt even after the children have come of age or the underlying criminal proceedings have terminated." Id.

62

Finally, DHA points to Rodriguez v. U.S. Department of the Army, 31 F. Supp. 3d 218 (D.D.C. 2014). Once again, that court had no occasion to interpret the statute's criminal-proceeding requirement; the underlying FOIA request sought records related to an investigation that resulted in a criminal prosecution and conviction. Id. at 273. So none of DHA's cited cases advances its cause.

63

Third, DHA points out that the Child Victims' Act imposes a confidentiality obligation on "any law enforcement agency involved in the case[.]" 18 U.S.C. § 3509(d)(1)(B)(i). Reasoning from this provision, DHA argues that "if no duty attached until a court proceeding commenced," "the requirement for investigative agencies to maintain confidentiality would be superfluous . . . because there would be nothing for a law enforcement agency involved in the case to keep secure."

64

Cross-Reply at 2-3. But of course, investigative agencies often retain records after a criminal prosecution concludes. So reading the Child Victims' Act to apply only to judicial proceedings does not defang the confidentiality obligations that the Act imposes on investigative agencies.

65

In sum, the Court is convinced that the term "criminal proceeding" in Section 3509 of the Child Victims' Act refers to criminal judicial proceedings, not merely criminal investigations. Cf.

66

Mid-Atl. Innocence Project, 2026 WL 775907, at *6 (holding that the Child Victims' Act "is inapplicable to 'criminal proceedings' held in State or local courts that ... are not federal courts subject to federal procedural and evidentiary rules"). Because DHA points to no qualifying "criminal proceeding" to which the withheld report relates, DHA cannot rely on Exemption 3 to withhold Dr. Brennan's report, and the Court need not reach the second prong of the Subsection 3509(d) analysis. Thus, the Court grants summary judgment to the Welters on Exemption 3.

67

B. Exemption 5

68

Next, DHA relies on Exemption 5 to redact "findings, opinions, and recommendations based on the personal opinions of the AFCCP multidisciplinary team" from Dr. Brennan's report.

69

Opp'n & Cross-Mot. at 13 (citing Lahiff Decl. "[ 28). Exemption 5 protects from disclosure "interagency or intraagency memorandums or letters that would not be available by law to a party other than an agency in litigation with the agency[.]" [5] U.S.C. § 552(b)(5). "To qualify under this exemption, a document must 'satisfy two conditions: its source must be a Government agency, and it must fall within the ambit of a privilege against discovery under judicial standards that would govern litigation against the agency that holds it." Welter v. U.S. Dep't of the Air Force, No. 22- cv-3738, 2026 WL 1243400, at 3 (D.D.C. May 6, 2026) (quoting Dep't of the Interior v. Klamath Water Users Protective Ass'n, 532 U.S. 1, 8 (2001)). Relevant here, Exemption 5 includes the deliberative-process privilege. Klamath Water Users, 532 U.S. at 8. "For a document to be covered by the deliberative process privilege, the document must be 'both predecisional and deliberative." Welter, 2026 WL 1243400, at 4 (quoting Reps. Comm. for

70

Freedom of the Press v. FBI, 3 F.4th 350, 362 (D.C. Cir. 2021)). "A document is predecisional if it was 'generated before the agency's final decision on the matter[.]" Reps. Comm., 3 F.4th at 362 (alteration in original) (quoting U.S. Fish & Wildlife Serv. v. Sierra Club, Inc., 592 U.S. 261, 268 (2021)). However, "a document can lose its predecisional character-and the protections of the privilege-if an agency adopts the document as its own." Jud. Watch, Inc. v. DOD, 847 F.3d 735, 739 (D.C. Cir. 2017). But "[t]o adopt a deliberative document, it is not enough for an agency to make vague or equivocal statements implying that a position presented in a deliberative document has merit; instead, the agency must make an 'express ' choice to use a deliberative document as a source of agency guidance." Id. (alteration and emphasis in original) (quoting NLRB v. Sears, Roebuck & Co., 421 U.S. 132, 161 (1975)). Meanwhile, "[a] document is deliberative when it is 'prepared to help the agency formulate its position[,]' and it 'reflects the give-and-take of the consultative process[.]" Reps. Comm., 3 F.4th at 362 (first quoting Sierra Club, 592 U.S. at 268; and then quoting Jud. Watch, Inc. v. FDA, 449 F.3d 141, 151 (D.C. Cir. 2006)). "In practice, these requirements 'tend to merge." Hall & Assocs. v. EPA, 633 F. Supp. 3d 35, 52 (D.D.C. 2022) (quoting Access Reps. v. DOJ, 926 F.2d 1192, 1195 (D.C. Cir. 1991)).

71

DHA invokes the deliberative process privilege to redact "analysis, findings, opinions, and recommendations[.]" Withholding Mem. at 11-12; see also id. at 6. In support of these redactions, Patrick L. Lahiff, an Associate General Counsel in DHA's Office of General Counsel, attests that Dr. Brennan's report was prepared "at the request of"' CID "as a part of a CID investigation . . . into allegations of sexual assault of the Welters' twin daughters by a third party, and allegations of child abuse of the Welters' twin daughters by Mr. and Mrs. Welter." Lahiff Decl. 14; see also id. 19 ("[T]he report was compiled for the express purpose of the CID's law enforcement investigation."). Mr. Lahiff further declares that "[t]he report's primary function was to provide

72

expert analysis of the medical information[,]" and that "[i]t contains the AFCCP's expert opinions, findings and recommendations to CID to help inform its law enforcement activities." Id. 1 10.

73

The Court is persuaded that DHA has adequately invoked the deliberative process privilege. The analysis and recommendations contained in the withheld report preceded CID's decision regarding whether and how to investigate the alleged abuse of the Welters' daughters. Id.

74

And Dr. Brennan prepared the report to aid CID in making those determinations. Id. 11 28-

75

Thus, the report was both predecisional and deliberative: it was "generated before the agency's

76

final decision on the matter" and "prepared to help the agency formulate its position." Sierra Club, 592 U.S. at 268.

77

The Welters argue that DHA has failed to establish that Dr. Brennan's report is

78

(1) predecisional and (2) deliberative. The Court disagrees.

79

The Welters first contend that the report is not predecisional because it was the final position of either DHA, Mot. at 12-13, or the Air Force, Reply & Cross-Opp'n at 7-8. But other than pointing to DHA's acknowledgment that the Air Force investigated the Welters "based on" the report, PSOF 1 11, they offer no reason to believe that either DHA or the Air Force "expressly adopt[ed]" the report or "incorporate[d] [it] by reference" into a final agency action, Sears, 421 U.S. at 161. Relatedly, the Welters allege that "[t]he report was shopped around by both Dr. Brennan and the Air Force's Family Advocacy Officer to various Child Protective Agencies, requesting they open investigations on the same[.]" Mot. at 13. And they say that "the Air Force used it to open and substantiate its own" investigation. Id. But the Welters do nothing to rebut DHA's showing that Dr. Brennan prepared the report to assist CID's decisionmaking. As the D.C.

80

Circuit has explained, "recommendations .. . suggesting a disposition of a particular case" that are "transmitted to superior authority for review and final action" qualify for the protection of the

81

deliberative process privilege. Coastal States Gas Corp. v. Dep't of Energy, 617 F.2d 854, 867 (D.C. Cir. 1980) (characterizing Renegotiation Bd. v. Grumman Aircraft Eng'g Corp., 421 U.S. 168 (1975)). That principle is dispositive here: DHA's unrebutted evidence establishes that Dr. Brennan's report contained analysis and recommendations designed to aid CID in its investigation. Thus, DHA properly withheld the report's analysis, opinions, and recommendations as predecisional.

82

Next, the Welters argue that Dr. Brennan's report is not deliberative because it contains "purely factual content[.]" Mot. at 13. Specifically, they note that DHA's withholding memorandum describes the report as "quot[ing] or describ[ing] ... medical information[.]" Withholding Mem. at 12. To be sure, the deliberative process privilege does not protect "[f]actual material that does not reveal the deliberative process[.]" Morley v. CIA, 508 F.3d 1108, 1127 (D.C.

83

Cir. 2007) (cleaned up). But "factual information is protected ... if its disclosure may so expose the deliberative process within an agency." Nat'l Ass'n of Minority Veterans v. U.S. Dep't of Veterans Affs., No. 21-cv-1298, 2024 WL 810032, at *10 (D.D.C. Feb. 27, 2024) (cleaned up).

84

And here, the factual medical information of the Welters' daughters was "assembled through an exercise of judgment in extracting pertinent material from a vast number of documents for the benefit of an official called upon to take discretionary action." Mapother v. DOJ, 3 F.3d 1533, 1539 (D.C. Cir. 1993).[4]

85

[4] Any factual medical information is also independently protected under Exemptions 6 and 7(C). See infra Discussion § C.

86

To the extent that the Welters intend to make a segregability challenge, that fails too.

87

DHA's declarant has attested that the agency "did not withhold any reasonable [sic] segregable, nonexempt portions" of the report and "conducted a line-by-line segregability analysis of the

88

exempt portions of the document[.]" Lahiff Decl. 11 19, 39. "Sworn agency declarations are afforded 'a presumption of good faith' in FOIA litigation." Leopold v. Fed. Hous. Fin. Agency, No. 23-cv-1935, 2026 WL 2676063, at *7 (D.D.C. Sep. 11, 2026) (quoting Shapiro v. DOJ, 944 F.3d 940, 943 (D.C. Cir. 2019)).

89

In sum, the Court concludes that DHA properly redacted portions of Dr. Brennan's report under Exemption 5. The Court grants summary judgment to DHA as to its Exemption 5 redactions.

90

C. Exemptions 6 and 7(C)

91

Finally, the Court considers DHA's Exemption 6 and Exemption 7(C) withholdings.

92

FOIA

93

Exemptions 6 and 7(C) both "seek to protect the privacy of individuals identified in certain agency records." ACLU v. DOJ, 655 F.3d 1, 6 (D.C. Cir. 2011). Exemption 6 permits an agency to withhold "personnel and medical files and similar files the disclosure of which would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy[.]" [5] U.S.C. § 552(b)(6). Exemption 7(C) protects "records or information compiled for law enforcement purposes, but only to the extent that the production of such law enforcement records or information ... could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy[.]" Id. § 552(b)(7)(C).

94

Because Exemption 7(C) permits the withholding of records "if disclosure would constitute an 'unwarranted' invasion of personal privacy, while Exemption 6 requires a 'clearly unwarranted' invasion to justify nondisclosure, Exemption 7(C) is more protective of privacy than Exemption 6 and thus establishes a lower bar for withholding material." ACLU, 655 F.3d at 6 (cleaned up). For that reason, when an agency claims that records may be withheld under both exemptions, a court "need only consider whether [the agency] properly invoked Exemption 7(C)." Id .; see also Reps.

95

Comm., 489 U.S. at 756 (noting that "7(C)'s privacy language is broader than the comparable language in Exemption 6 in two respects": (1) it does not require an invasion of privacy to be

96

"clearly" unwarranted, just "unwarranted"; and (2) it "encompasses any disclosure that 'could reasonably be expected to constitute' such an invasion" (emphasis added) (quoting 5 U.S.C.

97

§ 552(b)(7)(C)). Thus, "the Court need only address whether the agency has properly withheld

98

these documents under Exemption 7(C), and there is no need to separately consider the higher bar of Exemption 6." Blixseth v. ICE, No. 19-cv-1292, 2020 WL 210732, at *5 (D.D.C. Jan. 14, 2020); see also Braga v. FBI, 910 F. Supp. 2d 258, 267 (D.D.C. 2012) (same). So the Court evaluates whether DHA properly invoked Exemption 7(C). It first determines whether the withheld portions of the report comprise "records or information compiled for law enforcement purposes" and next considers whether their disclosure "could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy[.]" [5] U.S.C. § 552(b)(7).

99

Law Enforcement Purposes

100

To invoke Exemption 7(C), an agency must make a "threshold showing that the records were compiled for law enforcement purposes." Boyd v. EOUSA, 87 F. Supp. 3d 58, 72 (D.D.C. 2015) (citing 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(7)(C)). In other words, the "records must generally be generated during the course of an investigation and involve the detection or punishment of violations of law."

101

Pearce v. Dep't of Army, No. 24-cv-520, 2025 WL 1905552, at *10 (D.D.C. July 10, 2025) (cleaned up). "[T]he focus is on how and under what circumstances the requested files were compiled, and whether the files sought relate to anything that can fairly be characterized as an enforcement proceeding." Jefferson v. DOJ., Off. of Pro. Resp., 284 F.3d 172, 176-77 (D.C. Cir. 2002) (cleaned up).

102

Here, Dr. Brennan's report was compiled for law enforcement purposes. Recall that DHA's declarant attests the report was "prepared . . . as a part of a CID investigation . .. into allegations of sexual assault of the Welters' twin daughters by a third party, and allegations of child abuse of

103

the Welters' twin daughters by Mr. and Mrs. Welter." Lahiff Decl. 14. "CID is a federal criminal law enforcement investigative organization[.]" DSOF 1 55. And the report is stored in CID's case tracking system. DSOF | 17. Exemption 7(C)'s statutory threshold requires nothing further.

104

In arguing otherwise, the Welters claim that CID's investigation focused on alleged sexual abuse by DODEA employees, rather than alleged medical abuse by Mrs. Welter. Reply & Cross- Opp'n at 6-7. They contend that because CID never investigated them for alleged medical abuse, id. at 6, DHA has not "articulate[d] the nexus between the object of the investigation and the report authored by Dr. Brennan[,]" and therefore cannot invoke Exemption 7(C), id. at 7 (citing Campbell

105

v. DOJ, 164 F.3d 20, 33 (D.C. Cir. 1998)). This argument is wrong on two fronts. For starters, it

106

contradicts DHA's declaration that CID was investigating both allegations of sexual assault by a third party and allegations of child abuse by the Welters. Lahiff Decl. 14. But even assuming that the Welters are correct that CID was only investigating the alleged sexual assault, the report would still be a record "compiled for law enforcement purposes[.]" [5] U.S.C. § 552(b)(7)(C). The object of the investigation has no bearing on the Exemption 7(C) statutory threshold.

107

Unwarranted Invasion of Privacy

108

"After clearing [the Exemption 7(C)] threshold, the agency faces a balancing test." Ryan

109

v. DOJ, No. 23-cv-3815, 2026 WL 2676048, at *8 (D.D.C. Sep. 11, 2026). "First, a court will

110

consider whether disclosure 'would compromise a substantial, as opposed to de minimis, privacy interest,' because '[i]f no significant privacy interest is implicated . . . FOIA demands disclosure."

111

Id. (alteration in original) (quoting Nat'l Ass'n of Retired Fed. Emps. v. Horner, 879 F.2d 873, 874 (D.C. Cir. 1989)). Second, the Court must balance any privacy interests against any "countervailing public interest in disclosure" asserted by the Plaintiffs. Boyd, 87 F. Supp. 3d at 72-

112

[pg. 17]

113

a. Privacy Interests

114

"In the case of records related to investigations by criminal law enforcement agencies, Exemption 7(C) takes into consideration the 'strong interest' of all individuals-suspects, witnesses, and investigators-'in not being associated unwarrantedly with alleged criminal activity." Rodriguez, 31 F. Supp. 3d at 231 (quoting Dunkelberger v. DOJ, 906 F.2d 779, 781 (D.C. Cir. 1990)). As courts in this District have put it, "the general rule is that any third-party identifying information contained in law-enforcement records is categorically exempt from disclosure." Cullen v. DHS, No. 20-cv-113, 2023 WL 5607425, at *5 (D.D.C. Aug. 30, 2023) (emphasis in original) (cleaned up); see also Nation Mag., Washington Bureau v. U.S. Customs Serv., 71 F.3d 885, 896 (D.C. Cir. 1995) ("[T]o the extent any information contained in 7(C) investigatory files would reveal the identities of individuals who are subjects, witnesses, or informants in law enforcement investigations, those portions of responsive records are categorically exempt from disclosure[.]").

115

Here, DHA has identified three privacy interests that would be implicated by disclosure of the redacted portions of Dr. Brennan's report. All three are cognizable under Exemption 7(C).

116

First, DHA invokes the privacy interests of the Welters' minor daughters. DHA's memorandum avers that the report "contains intimate, detailed medical information concerning the children; details concerning the alleged sexual assault; and analysis of the children's medical information relating to the alleged child abuse and sexual assault." Withholding Mem. at 9. That type of third-party privacy interest is plainly sufficient under Exemption 7(C). See, e.g., Rodriguez, 31 F. Supp. 3d at 234 (explaining in the context of Exemption 7(C) that "privacy interests are at their apex" when the statements at issue "detail the sexual abuse of a minor"); Accurso v. FBI,

117

No. 19-cv-2540, 2021 WL 411152, at *8 (D.D.C. Feb. 5, 2021) ("[V]ictims' names properly are withheld under Exemption 7(C).").

118

Second, DHA seeks to shield the identities of the report's author and a CID agent involved with the investigation. See Withholding Mem. at 9-10. These are also cognizable privacy interests under Exemption 7(C). See, e.g., Lazaridis v. DOJ, 766 F. Supp. 2d 134, 144 (D.D.C. 2011) ("[T]he names of law enforcement officers who work on criminal investigations have usually been protected against release by exemption 7(C)."); Schrecker v. DOJ, 349 F.3d 657, 666 (D.C. Cir. 2003) (holding that "investigating agents ... have a substantial interest in seeing that their participation remains secret" (cleaned up)); Kimberlin v. DOJ, 139 F.3d 944, 949 (D.C. Cir. 1998) (recognizing the privacy interest of a government line attorney).

119

Third, and finally, DHA invokes Exemption 7(C) to protect the information of third-party providers described in the report. Withholding Mem. at 10. That interest, too, suffices for Exemption 7(C) purposes. See, e.g., Nation Mag., 71 F.3d at 894 (recognizing a privacy interest for "third parties who may be mentioned in investigatory files"); see also Martin, 488 F.3d at 457 (same).

120

b. Public Interest

121

On the other side of the scale-the "countervailing public interest in disclosure" furthered by the FOIA request, Boyd, 87 F. Supp. 3d at 72-73-the Welters rely entirely on a theory of "apparent wrongdoing" by DHA. Mot. at 11. "[W]here ... the public interest being asserted" in an Exemption 7(C) case "is to show that responsible officials acted negligently or otherwise improperly in the performance of their duties, the requester . . . must produce evidence that would warrant a belief by a reasonable person that the alleged Government impropriety might have

122

occurred." Nat'l Archives & Recs. Admin. v. Favish, 541 U.S. 157, 174 (2004). This standard is "demanding[.]" Blackwell v. FBI, 646 F.3d 37, 41 (D.C. Cir. 2011).

123

The Welters do not clear this lofty bar. They first speculate that "the purpose of Dr. Brennan's report may have been to shy away from allegations of sexual abuse by DODEA employees in Germany[,]" citing a sexual-abuse conviction of a DODEA schoolteacher in Stuttgart during the same period as their daughters' alleged sexual abuse. Mot. at 10. They also note that the report's author expressed an inability to access their daughters' medical records-records that the Welters say the author should have been able to access. See Mot. at 10-11. These two theories, the Welters urge, "present some evidence that DHA, knowing Dr. Brennan's report is faulty, is attempting to shield it from disclosure." Mot. at 11. But the Welters present nothing to back up their claim of wrongdoing. Weighing this meager showing of public interest against the strong protection that Exemption 7(C) affords to third-party information, there is no doubt that DHA's withholdings were proper under Exemption 7(C). See Rodriguez, 31 F. Supp. 3d at 233 ("If there is a privacy interest in the requested materials and no public interest in disclosure, '[the court] need not linger over the balance; something, even a modest privacy interest, outweighs nothing every time." (quoting Horner, 879 F.2d at 879).

124

In sum, DHA has sufficiently supported its Exemption 7(C) withholdings. Moreover, the Government would prevail even under Exemption 6's higher threshold. Cf. Blixseth, 2020 WL 210732, at *6. Accordingly, the Court will grant summary judgment to DHA as to Exemption 6 and 7(C).[5]

125

D. In Camera Review

126

The Welters urge the Court to review Dr. Brennan's report in camera to determine the propriety of DHA's withholdings. Mot. at 14-15; Reply & Cross-Opp'n at 8. But the D.C. Circuit has warned that "[w]hen the agency meets its burden by means of affidavits," in camera review "is neither necessary nor appropriate." Hayden v. NSA, 608 F.2d 1381, 1387 (D.C. Cir. 1979). So in camera review is inappropriate here.

127

CONCLUSION

128

For the foregoing reasons, the Court grants in part and denies in part the Plaintiffs' Motion for Summary Judgment, ECF No. 17, and the Defendant's Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment, ECF No. 20. The Defendant may not withhold the report in question in full under Exemption 3, but it has justified its redactions under Exemptions 5, 6, and 7(C).

129

A separate order will issue.

A new clinic at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson is expanding healthcare options for women experiencing perimenopause and menopause.
The 673rd Medical Group recently opened the Women’s Mid-Life Optimizations Direct Access Clinic, offering services such as diagnostic lab testing and hormone therapy to help patients manage symptoms linked to hormonal changes.

Patients can start the screening process by visiting or calling the Women’s Health Clinic. After an initial screening and lab testing, eligible patients will be contacted about two weeks later to schedule an in-person appointment.

I heard this so many times.

Commanders, NCOS, 30+ year vets who were on lifetime Tricare. Every time I thought to myself, “99% of Americans seem to be figuring it out... what am I missing?”

It turns out not much. (And if you want to hear more, check out our transition 101 webinar Nov 4 at Sitreps dot com / webinars. Stephen Spake, my former platoon sergeant turned health care guru will be diving into this)

Don’t get me wrong, healthcare coverage and affordability in the US can and should improve (I’ll leave the debate on how for another thread, maybe on X lol).

But... 82% of Americans at present report that they are overall satisfied with their healthcare coverage. Which contrasts sharply with the hellscape that commanders and field grades claimed I would walk into should I decide to leave.

So, what are realistic costs?

That depends on a few things. If you’re in the reserves or National Guard your Tricare premiums are roughly $280/ month for your entire family. If you’re 100% disabled, your family has champva capped at $3K/year.

The average employee with a family of four will pay roughly $9-$12K total per year in the US. About $7K of that monthly premiums and the rest out of pocket deductibles and uncovered costs.

Is that worse than free? Yeah, sure. But for most people getting out they should ask if they’d stay in if branch called and offered a $10K per year bonus. I think we all know instinctively what that answer would be.

text:
Beginning January 1, 2027, TRICARE will launch a five-year pilot program to test separate payments for blood products administered by EMS agencies. The initiative seeks to address financial gaps that currently complicate the delivery of life-saving transfusions to trauma patients before they arrive at a hospital.

Why it matters

Uncontrolled bleeding from traumatic injuries remains a primary cause of preventable death, yet current bundled ambulance payments rarely cover the high cost of blood products. This pilot aims to incentivize agencies to expand access to prehospital blood therapy by providing a dedicated funding mechanism for the resources and maintenance required.

Blood product costs currently range from $500 to $925 per unit, and trauma accounts for 80% of documented blood-treatment responses. While air units performed 87% of administrations in 2025, ground units handled the remaining 10%.

The players

TRICARE

This is the healthcare program serving uniformed service members, retirees, and their families around the world.

Hillsborough County Fire Rescue

This Florida-based agency provides emergency response and fire services, including recent innovations in drone technology for medical logistics.

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services

This federal agency manages health programs and recently adjusted payment categories for ground-ambulance services.

America's Blood Centers

This organization represents community-based, non-profit blood centers that collect and supply blood products across the nation.

The details

Most current EMS agencies do not stock blood due to high costs and storage requirements, despite the significant survival benefits for trauma victims. To improve response times, Hillsborough County Fire Rescue recently demonstrated a drone program capable of delivering blood products to scenes in under four minutes.

Timeline

September 4, 2025: John Mazanec was injured in a motorcycle wreck in Pueblo, Colorado.

October 1, 2026: Hillsborough County demonstrated a drone blood-delivery program.

January 1, 2027: The TRICARE pilot program for blood payment begins.

December 31, 2031: The five-year TRICARE pilot program concludes.

Related coverage

Philanthropy

Oct. 21

American Red Cross Urges Blood and Platelet Donations

Stroke

Oct. 21

Bleeding Stroke Patients Face Slower Hospital Care

Market Landscape

The TRICARE pilot follows the 2025 Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services move to shift transfusions into higher ground-ambulance payment categories. This development suggests a broader industry shift toward formalizing prehospital blood delivery as a standard, reimbursable component of emergency care.

This policy change is designed to increase the availability of life-saving blood products for patients in rural or hard-to-reach areas during emergencies. For the average citizen, this could lead to faster and more advanced medical interventions during critical ambulance responses.

The takeaway

The move toward standardized reimbursement for blood products reflects an urgent need to treat trauma in the field before patients reach a hospital. Communities should monitor whether local EMS agencies begin stocking blood supplies as these federal payment structures are implemented.

What happens next

The pilot program is scheduled to commence on January 1, 2027, and will continue operations through December 31, 2031.

title: After a crash, can blood reach you in time? | Health | wyomingnews.com
description: ImageTrend reports that receiving blood before reaching a hospital is far from universally available.
text:
Alicia Raebel was grocery shopping with her three sons when a crash-alert service called. Her husband, John Mazanec, had been in a motorcycle wreck. He was not answering his phone.
After a truck turned across his path in Pueblo, Colorado, on Sept. 4, 2025, paramedics found him bleeding heavily. Another crew brought blood from the ambulance company's base, and his transfusion began on the way to the hospital. The local program had launched just eight days earlier, according to
an August 2026 account published by UCHealth
.

"Had they not started me on the blood, I don't think I would be here," Mazanec told UCHealth.
Mazanec's case is one example of a treatment occurring across the country. Drawing on a representative sample of U.S. EMS incidents,
ImageTrend's
2026 EMS Insights Report
documented 1,695 crash patients receiving blood before hospital arrival in 2025. Those cases offer a broader picture of how blood reaches patients.
But receiving blood before reaching a hospital is far from universally available.
America's Blood Centers
, an association representing independent blood centers, estimates that only 1% to 2% of EMS agencies nationwide carry blood.
Starting Jan. 1, 2027,
TRICARE
, the health program for service members, retirees and their families, will test whether paying ambulance providers separately for blood products and transfusion services improves access and patient outcomes for eligible beneficiaries.
Who receives blood before reaching the hospital
Across the report's blood-treatment records, 80% of responses involved trauma, 44% of recipients were ages 20 to 49 and 68% were recorded as male. Nearly 2 in 5 recipients were injured in traffic or motorcycle crashes.
ImageTrend, Source: ImageTrend 2026 EMS Insights Report, page 15.
For a severely injured patient, waiting until hospital arrival can mean continuing to lose blood during the ride. Uncontrolled bleeding from traumatic injuries is a leading cause of preventable death, according to the
American College of Surgeons
, and a significant loss can become fatal within minutes.
Giving blood before hospital arrival, called prehospital blood transfusion, allows responders to begin replacing what a patient has lost. A
2025 clinical practice guideline
from the Prehospital Blood Transfusion Coalition supports early transfusion for patients in hemorrhagic shock, when blood loss leaves the body unable to maintain adequate circulation.
Blood is not needed for every crash injury. Clinicians select patients using medical protocols, and a transfusion cannot replace bleeding control or surgery to repair internal injuries.
How blood reaches patients depends on the local response
According to the EMS Insights Report, in 2025, air units performed 87% of the report's documented blood administrations, while ground units performed 10%. These figures include emergencies beyond crashes.
Across the blood-treatment records, 42% of responses occurred in rural counties. Ground-unit transfusions were more concentrated in urban counties, where 77% took place.
In the report's motor-vehicle-crash analysis, blood was recorded in 0.67% of rural EMS activations, compared with 0.08% in metro areas.
For someone injured on a road outside town, or on a city street, those findings raise a practical question: Which crew could bring blood to the scene or administer it during the trip to a hospital?
An emergency blood program does not require every ambulance to carry blood. The
federal Office of EMS
describes regional programs in which 911 centers can dispatch blood resources to an emergency. One crew can bring blood to another already treating a patient, as happened in Mazanec's case.
That means the estimate that only 1% to 2% of EMS agencies carry blood tells just part of the story. A crew that doesn't stock blood may still be able to get it from another responding unit. Counting agencies alone cannot show which communities have access or how quickly blood can reach a patient.
The cost of keeping blood ready for the next emergency
A donated unit of blood needs a system to collect it, prepare it and make it available for treatment. America's Blood Centers says blood product
costs can run $500 to $925 or more per unit
. The association argues that bundled ambulance payments do not adequately cover those costs.
Ambulance programs also need temperature-monitored coolers, equipment to warm blood for transfusion and trained clinicians. Arrangements with blood suppliers and hospitals must cover replenishment and unused products. Keeping that service ready creates expenses even between emergencies.
A payment pilot will test a way to expand access
The
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
moved transfusions into a higher ground-ambulance payment category in 2025, but blood remains bundled into the transport payment.
Under
a federal notice published in July
, TRICARE providers will be able to bill separately for medically necessary blood products and transfusion services during qualifying transports for eligible beneficiaries. The five-year pilot runs through Dec. 31, 2031, and will assess access, outcomes and costs.
Communities are exploring new ways to deliver blood
In Florida, a new demonstration explores delivery by air without an ambulance helicopter. On Oct. 1, 2026, Hillsborough County Fire Rescue
demonstrated a drone blood-delivery program
intended to bring a temperature-controlled unit of whole blood directly to an emergency scene at a paramedic's request.
The initial service is planned for two areas of unincorporated Hillsborough County covering 70 square miles. The department projects three and a half minutes or less from request to blood administration. That is a performance target, rather than a reported result from patient care.
The county's October announcement said live operations were expected in the coming weeks, with the first year serving as a proof of concept.
By tackling delivery times and financing, the drone program and reimbursement pilot address different parts of the same life-or-death problem: getting blood to a patient while it can still save them.
Residents can help before the next emergency
A useful question for your local EMS agency is whether blood can reach a severely bleeding patient before hospital arrival. Ask how it gets there and how the service is supported. That opens a more useful conversation than asking only whether one ambulance carries blood.
Blood donation supports the supply that hospitals and ambulance programs depend on.
Contact a local blood center about eligibility and appointments
. The federal Office of EMS identifies blood-bank partnerships and community blood drives as ways to support programs.
Residents can also learn bleeding control through the American College of Surgeons'
Stop the Bleed training
, which teaches direct pressure, wound packing and appropriate tourniquet use. If you encounter a crash, protect your own safety, call 911 and follow dispatcher instructions.
Mazanec underwent surgeries and rehabilitation. By summer 2026, he was fishing again with his wife and sons, UCHealth reported.
The transfusion was an early step in a long recovery. Making that step possible for another family requires blood donors, trained responders and a way to sustain the service before the next emergency begins.
About the research
ImageTrend used Collaborate data, an opt-in
nationally representative dataset of de-identified EMS records
from more than 3,100 organizations. The
2026 EMS Insights Report
identifies blood treatment through procedure and medication records, however, documentation practices may vary by agency.
This story was produced by
ImageTrend
and reviewed and distributed by
Stacker
.

text:
Nothing in the Department of Justice’s $1.8 billion health care fraud takedown in Los Angeles stops at the United States border. One of the defendants in the sweep announced on Thursday, October 22, is a Filipino American nurse accused of spending part of a $906 million Medicare and Tricare scheme on a beach resort in Cagayan province.

The photograph shows the Edward R. Roybal Federal Building and US Courthouse in downtown Los Angeles, where the federal cases were announced. It was taken in April 2022 and does not depict the takedown, any defendant or any beneficiary. (Photo: Busition, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

Marizel Yukee, a nurse practitioner from Nevada, was indicted in June in the Southern District of Texas. Prosecutors say she owned and ran four wound care companies in Texas, Nevada, California and Hawaii and billed for skin graft procedures that were never needed.

This story is about the wider sweep announced on October 22. It does not report any new charge against Yukee.

Her case is not part of the 15 defendants announced this week. It is the same federal campaign, run through the same Justice Department fraud division, and it is the part of the crackdown with a Philippine asset attached.

What prosecutors say Yukee did

According to the indictment filed on June 18 in Houston, Yukee and unnamed accomplices submitted about $906 million in claims to Medicare and Tricare between October 2023 and April 2025.

The claims were for allografts, tissue transplants that prosecutors describe as medically unnecessary. The filing says Yukee billed an average of more than $1 million per patient and that the government paid out about $297 million.

Prosecutors say she ignored Medicare’s rule on reporting the true invoice price of the grafts and instead billed far higher amounts. An email quoted in the indictment reportedly shows her telling colleagues to inflate prices.

Two companies acting as allograft distributors allegedly paid her nearly $16 million in kickbacks to push their products, and the indictment describes a network of referral and purchasing payments around the wound care businesses.

The Philippine property and the seizure

Federal prosecutors say part of the money went into a lifestyle that includes a multi-million dollar home in Hawaii, a Bulgari necklace valued at $865,000, a Ferrari worth $594,000, and the development of a $4.6 million resort in Santa Ana, Cagayan.

The US government has since seized $30 million in bank accounts, luxury cars and jewelry valued at nearly $2 million, the Department of Justice announced in June.

Item Detail per the Department of Justice Defendant Marizel Yukee, nurse practitioner, Nevada Where charged Southern District of Texas, Houston, indictment filed June 18, 2026 Claims submitted About $906 million to Medicare and Tricare, October 2023 to April 2025 Government payout About $297 million Alleged kickbacks received Nearly $16 million from two allograft distributors Assets seized $30 million in accounts, cars and jewelry worth nearly $2 million Philippine asset named $4.6 million beach resort in Santa Ana, Cagayan

Why it landed in the same week as the bigger sweep

The October 22 announcement in Los Angeles covered 15 defendants, including six medical professionals, and about $1.8 billion in allegedly fraudulent claims. Eight people were arrested that day.

The largest piece is a $1.6 billion scheme that prosecutors say trafficked vulnerable people across the country for sham substance abuse treatment. Another case charges an Anaheim heart surgeon and a Tarzana chiropractor over about $135 million in unnecessary artery procedures.

Justice Department officials framed the round as part of a wider push against benefits fraud, citing a $25 million whistleblower program announced by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance two days earlier. The department says its health care fraud strike forces have charged more than 6,200 defendants since 2007.

The Los Angeles Times reported that California Attorney General Rob Bonta and First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli held competing news conferences the same morning, each claiming credit for the arrests. Bonta said state investigators made the arrest of the Anaheim surgeon.

What this means for Filipino families

For readers in the Philippines, the Cagayan resort is the detail that makes this a local story. A criminal judgment from a Texas court can, in principle, reach property acquired with proceeds traced to the fraud, including property abroad, though no Philippine court has been asked to act in this case and no forfeiture of the resort has been reported.

The practical warning is about recruitment, not prosecution. Prosecutors say both Yukee’s alleged scheme and the hospice cases in Los Angeles worked through the same door: trusted intermediaries signing up elderly patients for services they did not need and often did not understand.

Filipino Americans are a large share of the US health care workforce. Earlier this month, this desk reported on Filipino nurses who won a $1.85 million US settlement over quit-fee contracts, and on a bill that would fine H-1B employers up to $250,000 for visa fraud.

What is not established

An indictment is an allegation. Yukee is presumed innocent, and none of the charges described here has been proved in court.

No source reviewed for this article shows a conviction, a sentence or a plea from Yukee in this case. The seizure announced in June is a court-authorised asset hold, not a finding of guilt.

No Philippine court filing, forfeiture order or agency action concerning the Santa Ana resort appears in any source reviewed. The $906 million figure is the amount allegedly billed, not an amount collected.
